segments.say: In 1999, a paper appeared in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology with one of the best titles in the field. It was called Unskilled and Unaware of It: How Difficulties in Recognizing One's Own Incompetence Lead to Inflated Self-Assessments. The authors were two psychologists at Cornell University, David Dunning and Justin Kruger.

show.title: The people who think they are above average

segments.say: The story of how they came to the idea is a good one. In 1995, a man named McArthur Wheeler robbed two banks in Pittsburgh in broad daylight, with his face covered in lemon juice. He believed that, because lemon juice is used as invisible ink, it would make him invisible to the cameras. He was arrested the same evening.

show.sub: A bank robber in lemon juice

segments.say: Dunning read about the case and asked himself an interesting question. It wasn't only that the man was wrong. It was that he was so confident. Could it be that the skills you need to do something well are the same skills you need to tell whether you're doing it well?

They tested this in four studies. Students at Cornell took short tests of humour, logical reasoning and English grammar. Afterwards, they were asked to estimate how well they had done, in comparison with others. Then the researchers compared each person's estimate with their actual score.

show.what: Students rated their own ability in humour, logic and grammar

segments.say: The pattern was striking. The students who scored in the bottom quarter, on average, rated themselves as above average, somewhere around the sixtieth percentile. Their real performance was much lower, around the twelfth. They weren't just wrong, they were wrong in a flattering direction.

show.title: The lowest scorers
show.label: estimated themselves at about the 60th percentile

segments.say: The best performers made the opposite mistake. The top quarter estimated themselves a little below their real position. Dunning and Kruger suggested that because the task was easy for them, they assumed it was easy for everyone else too. They weren't lacking confidence. They simply thought others were as good as they were.

These figures are rounded and based on the paper's first study. The most important thing to notice is that, although everyone guessed in the middle to upper range, the real scores were widely spread. Those who knew the least had the least information about how much there was to know.

Dunning and Kruger called it a double burden. People who lack skill make mistakes, and then can't recognise them. And there was a hopeful second half of the story. In one of their studies, they gave poor performers a short training course in logical reasoning. After it, the participants became much better at judging how badly they had done before.

That might be the most useful finding of all. Getting better doesn't only make you more skilled, it makes you better at seeing your limits. Think of the beginner who says that they don't know how little they know, and the expert who says that the more they learn, the more there is to learn.

show.sub: Learning shows you what you don't know

segments.say: You may have met a graph that's circulated online. It has a peak of confidence at the start, a deep valley of doubt, and a slow climb after that. It's called the Dunning-Kruger curve, and it's very popular. But it's worth knowing that it doesn't come from the original paper.

That's a fair summary. The original finding was a more modest one than the memes suggest. The bottom group overestimated, the top group slightly underestimated, and everyone was better at spotting skill in others once they'd learned it themselves. There was no claim that stupid people are the most sure of everything.

show.title: What the popular version gets wrong
items: The famous mountain-and-valley curve is not in the 1999 paper
The paper didn't say that fools are the most confident people
It showed a gap between estimates and results
The gap was biggest at low skill

segments.say: Like every study in this video, this one has been challenged. And in this case, the criticisms are interesting, because some of them are about statistics. In the 2000s and 2010s, several researchers argued that part of the pattern could appear for reasons that have nothing to do with skill or self-awareness.

One argument is that when you plot people's own estimates against their scores, you will tend to see the bottom group overestimate and the top group underestimate, even if the data were random. This is a statistical effect known as regression to the mean, along with a general tendency for people to rate themselves as above average.

Dunning and others have answered that the basic effect holds even when you control for these things. And studies in the years since, across different tasks and countries, have found that people with low skill generally overestimate how well they've done. But how much of the pattern is true self-blindness, and how much is statistical, is still debated.

show.sub: Part of the pattern is real

segments.say: There's also evidence that people are not hopeless at judging themselves. In many tasks, people's estimates track their real ability to a moderate degree. We're better judges of ourselves in areas where we get quick, clear feedback, such as sports, and worse where feedback is vague, such as leadership, humour or social skills.

That makes sense. If you shoot a basketball, you immediately see if it goes in. But if you tell a joke, or give a speech, or manage a team, the feedback can be mixed, delayed or polite. And so our picture of ourselves can drift away from the facts, in either direction.

show.title: Where we misjudge most
show.label: where feedback is slow, rare or unclear

segments.say: It's also worth saying that the effect isn't about other people. Each of us is a beginner at most things, and in those areas we are all likely to be a bit too sure or a bit too unsure. A kinder way of reading the research is that blind spots are normal, and the sensible response is to go and look for them.
None of these is complicated. And the most important one might be the last. The feeling of certainty isn't evidence. It's a feeling, and it can be as strong when we're wrong as when we're right.

show.title: Ways to see your blind spots
items: Ask for specific feedback from someone you trust
Test yourself against a clear standard
Learn a little more about the field
Notice when you feel certain and rarely check

segments.say: Glasses, a mirror and a book, an odd little still life, and yet it describes the whole idea. To see ourselves clearly, we need something to look through, something to look into, and something to learn from. Self-knowledge is a skill, and like any skill, it improves with practice.

show.cap: Glasses, a mirror, an open book

segments.say: We've covered a lot of ground. We began with a child and a marshmallow, and ended with a robber and some lemon juice. In between, we met rooms full of people giving wrong answers, a calm voice asking others to go on, a doll, two mothers made of wire and cloth, a crowd, a hospital ward, a dog, a baby, a forgotten list, a basement and a boring task.

That's a long list, and it's quite a human one. These aren't really lessons about strange laboratories. They're about the ordinary things we do every day, among people we know. And they're a good reminder that psychology is a conversation, not a set of final answers.

show.title: Twelve experiments, twelve lessons
items: Waiting: self-control depends on trust and context
Asch: one ally can break the group's spell
Milgram: authority is powerful, and so is refusing
Bobo: children learn by watching
Harlow: comfort is a need
Bystanders: say it out loud, ask one person
Rosenhan: labels distort what we see
Pavlov: what's learned can be unlearned
Ebbinghaus: space it out, test yourself
Stanford: roles are not destiny
Festinger: we justify what we do
Dunning and Kruger: look for your blind spots

segments.say: If there is one thread that ties them together, it's that we aren't isolated minds. We watch, we copy, we belong, we justify, we label and we are labelled. We're shaped by the rooms we're in and the people in them. And, at the same time, we have more choice than we often think.

There's a second thread, and it's a more sobering one. Many of the most famous experiments in psychology have been challenged, corrected or complicated, from the marshmallow test to the Stanford basement. That doesn't make psychology worthless. It makes it a science that notices its own mistakes, which is how a science should be.

So the habit I'd suggest is this: when you hear that a study has proved something about human nature, ask who was studied, how big the study was, whether anyone has repeated it, and what the effect really was. It takes only a moment, and it protects you against a great many confident headlines.

And there's a gentle habit too. If we know that situations pull on people, that labels distort, that groups press and that confidence misleads, we can afford to be a little kinder, to others and to ourselves. Most of us are doing the best we can, in rooms we didn't design.

If you would like to take something away, pick one experiment, and one small habit, and try it this week. Write down what you want to remember and test yourself tomorrow. Be the ally in a meeting. Ask a stranger if they're okay. Look twice before you label someone. Small things, repeated gently, are how people change.

Before we finish, it's worth asking which of the twelve stayed with you most. Was it the quiet power of one ally in the room of wrong answers? The reminder that a baby needs comfort as well as food? The idea that our reasons for doing things are sometimes written after the fact? The one that lingers is probably the one that touches something in your own life, and that is a good place to start thinking.

Thank you for spending this time with me. If any of these stories surprised you, you're welcome to tell me which one, and which experiment you'd like us to look at next. There are many more waiting, and some of them are even stranger than these.
That's all for now. Sleep well, stay curious, and I'll see you in the next one.
